objects.name: Hoag's Object
objects.why: A nearly perfect ring of young blue stars around a round, yellow core, with a gap between them that looks almost empty. Through the gap, by pure chance, another, much more distant ring galaxy can be seen.
unknown: How the ring formed. A collision normally leaves a lopsided ring, not this symmetric one; the other ideas — a small galaxy shredded and spread round, or gas falling in from intergalactic space — haven't been settled.
Why the gap between the core and the ring is so empty.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0424 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Hoag's Object is an unusual ring galaxy in the constellation of Serpens Caput. It is named after Arthur Hoag, who discovered it in 1950 and identified it as either a planetary nebula or a peculiar galaxy. The galaxy has a D25 isophotal diameter of 45.41 kiloparsecs (148,000 light-years).

objects.name: NGC 4650A
objects.why: A polar-ring galaxy: an old, flattened galaxy with a ring of gas and young stars circling over its poles, at right angles to its main body.
unknown: Whether the ring came from a merger or collision, or from gas flowing in along an intergalactic filament.
The shape of its dark-matter halo: the ring and the body orbit in different planes, so they probe the halo in two directions at once, and studies disagree about how flattened it is.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: NGC 4650A is a lenticular galaxy of the rare polar-ring type, located in the southern constellation of Centaurus. It has an apparent visual magnitude of 13.3 and spans an angular size of 1.6′ × 0.8′. This galaxy is located at an estimated distance of 130 million light-years (39.8 Mpc) and is receding with a heliocentric radial velocity of 2,908.5 km/s. It should not be confused with the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 4650; the physical distance between both galaxies is only about 6 times the optical radius of NGC 4650. NGC 4650A lies in a chain of five galaxies in the Centaurus Cluster.

objects.name: NGC 1052-DF2
objects.why: An ultra-diffuse galaxy about as wide as the Milky Way but with roughly 200 times fewer stars. Its globular clusters move so slowly that it seemed to contain little or no dark matter (van Dokkum et al. 2018) — strange, since dark matter is thought to be what holds galaxies together as they form.
unknown: Its distance: about 20 Mpc by one method, about 13 Mpc by another (Trujillo et al. 2019) — and at the nearer distance it would have a normal amount of dark matter.
If it really lacks dark matter, how it formed. One idea is a high-speed collision of two gas-rich dwarf galaxies, in which the gas was stopped and the dark matter carried on.
objects.distSrc: published values disagree: about 13 Mpc (Trujillo et al. 2019) against about 20–22 Mpc (van Dokkum et al. 2018; Shen et al. 2021); 20 Mpc shown
objects.about: NGC 1052-DF2 is an ultra diffuse galaxy (UDG) identified in a wide-field imaging survey of the NGC 1052 group by the Dragonfly Telephoto Array. It has been proposed that the galaxy contains little or no dark matter, the first such discovery. On 20 March 2019, a follow-up study announcing the discovery of a second UDG lacking dark matter, NGC 1052-DF4, was published.

objects.name: NGC 1052-DF4
objects.why: A second faint galaxy in the same group as NGC 1052-DF2 that also appears to have very little dark matter (2019).
unknown: Whether its large neighbour NGC 1035 stripped its dark matter away — faint tidal tails were reported around it in 2020.
Whether DF2 and DF4 were born in the same collision, which would also have left a line of similar dark-matter-poor galaxies (proposed in 2022).
objects.distSrc: about 20 Mpc from its brightest red-giant stars (Danieli et al. 2020)
objects.about: NGC 1052-DF2 is an ultra diffuse galaxy (UDG) identified in a wide-field imaging survey of the NGC 1052 group by the Dragonfly Telephoto Array. It has been proposed that the galaxy contains little or no dark matter, the first such discovery. On 20 March 2019, a follow-up study announcing the discovery of a second UDG lacking dark matter, NGC 1052-DF4, was published.

objects.name: NGC 1569
objects.why: A small irregular galaxy in the middle of a starburst — making stars far faster than a galaxy its size normally does — with giant young star clusters and hot gas being blown out of it.
unknown: What set off the burst: an encounter with a neighbour or gas falling in are suspected.

Its distance: a 2008 study put it at about 11 million light-years, further than many earlier estimates (the distance shown is the median of all published values, old and new) — and the further away, the more intense the burst.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: NGC 1569 is a dwarf irregular galaxy in Camelopardalis. The galaxy is relatively nearby, and consequently, the Hubble Space Telescope can easily resolve the stars within the galaxy. The distance to the galaxy was previously believed to be only 2.4 Mpc. However, in 2008 scientists studying images from Hubble calculated the galaxy's distance at nearly 11 million light-years away, about 4 million light-years farther than previously thought, meaning it is a member of the IC 342 group of galaxies.

objects.name: IC 1101
objects.why: The giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of the galaxy cluster Abell 2029, often listed among the largest galaxies known.
unknown: How big it really is: its faint outer halo fades into the cluster's own diffuse starlight, so where the galaxy 'ends' is a matter of definition, and quoted sizes vary hugely.
Why its core is so large and faint — possibly stars flung out by a pair of supermassive black holes spiralling together.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: IC 1101 is a class S0 supergiant (cD) lenticular galaxy at the center of the Abell 2029 galaxy cluster. It has an isophotal diameter at about 123.65 to 169.61 kiloparsecs. It possesses a diffuse core, which is the largest core of any galaxy known to date, and contains a supermassive black hole, one of the largest discovered.

objects.name: NGC 1277
objects.why: A small, dense, old galaxy in the Perseus cluster that seems to have stopped changing about 10 billion years ago — a 'relic' of the early universe that never merged with anything.
unknown: Its central black hole was first reported (2012) as one of the most massive known for its galaxy's size; later measurements revised it down, and the true value is still argued.
A 2023 study found little sign of dark matter in its inner regions, which is hard to explain for a galaxy like this.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: NGC 1277 is a lenticular galaxy in the constellation of Perseus. It is a member of the Perseus Cluster of galaxies and is located approximately 73 Mpc (megaparsecs) or 240 million light-years from the Milky Way. It has an apparent magnitude of about 14.7. It was discovered on December 4, 1875, by Lawrence Parsons, 4th Earl of Rosse.

objects.name: Dragonfly 44
objects.why: An ultra-diffuse galaxy in the Coma cluster, about as wide as the Milky Way but with around 1% of its stars, found with the Dragonfly telescope array.
unknown: How much dark matter it has: early measurements suggested it is almost all dark matter; later studies of its stars and globular clusters disagree.
Whether ultra-diffuse galaxies are 'failed' Milky Ways that stopped making stars early, or ordinary dwarfs puffed up.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0213 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Dragonfly 44 is an ultra diffuse galaxy in the Coma Cluster. This galaxy is well-known because observations of the velocity dispersion in 2016 suggested a mass of about one trillion solar masses, about the same as the Milky Way. This mass was consistent with a count of about 90 and 70 globular clusters observed around Dragonfly 44 in two different studies.

objects.name: Malin 1
objects.why: A giant, extremely faint spiral found by accident in 1986. Its dim disk is several times wider than the Milky Way's.
unknown: How such a huge, thin, faint disk formed and survived: collisions, slow accretion of gas over billions of years, and formation in a very empty region have all been proposed.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0827 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Malin 1 is a giant low surface brightness (LSB) spiral galaxy in the constellation Coma Berenices. It is located 1.19 billion light-years (366 Mpc) away near the North Galactic Pole, and is one of the largest known spiral galaxies, with an approximate diameter of 650,000 light-years (200,000 pc); this makes Malin 1 over six times the diameter of our Milky Way. It was discovered by astronomer David Malin in 1986, from which it derives its name, and is the first LSB galaxy verified to exist. Its bright center, an SB0a-type barred-spiral, is 30,000 light-years (9,200 pc) across, with a bulge of 10,000 light-years (3,100 pc).

objects.name: Cartwheel Galaxy
objects.why: A ring galaxy made when a smaller galaxy plunged through the middle of a spiral a few hundred million years ago. The collision sent a wave outward like a ripple in a pond, and it set off a ring of star formation.
unknown: Which of the small galaxies nearby was the one that hit it.
How its 'spokes' formed and how the galaxy will settle down.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0302 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: The Cartwheel Galaxy (catalogue ESO 350-40 and PGC 2248) is a lenticular ring galaxy around 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor. It has a D25 isophotal diameter of 57.69 kiloparsecs (188,200 light-years), and a mass of about 2.9–4.8 billion solar masses; its outer ring has a circular velocity of 217 km/s.

objects.name: Antennae Galaxies
objects.why: Two spiral galaxies in the middle of colliding, with two long curved tails of stars flung out by tides and thousands of newly formed star clusters.
unknown: Its distance has been disputed — about 45 versus about 72 million light-years — which changes how bright and massive its young clusters are.
How many of the young star clusters will survive to become long-lived globular clusters.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Antennae Galaxies are a pair of interacting galaxies in the constellation Corvus. They are currently going through a starburst phase, in which the collision of clouds of gas and dust, with entangled magnetic fields, causes rapid star formation. They were discovered by William Herschel in 1785.

objects.name: The Mice
objects.why: Two galaxies early in a merger, each trailing a long tail of stars — the reason for the name. They are expected to become one elliptical galaxy.
unknown: Exactly how long the merger will take and what will be left; this pair is a standard test for computer simulations of mergers.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0220 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: NGC 4676, or the Mice Galaxies, are two spiral galaxies in the constellation Coma Berenices. About 105.8 megaparsecs distant, they have begun the process of colliding and merging. Their "mice" name refers to the long tails produced by tidal action—the relative difference between gravitational pulls on the near and far parts of each galaxy—known here as a galactic tide. It is a possibility that both galaxies, which are members of the Coma Cluster, have experienced a collision, and will continue colliding until they coalesce.

objects.name: Arp 220
objects.why: The nearest ultra-luminous infrared galaxy: two galaxies merging, their two nuclei buried in dust and forming stars at a furious rate.
unknown: How much of its enormous infrared light comes from star formation and how much from black holes growing out of sight behind the dust.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0184 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Arp 220 is the result of a collision between two galaxies which are now in the process of merging. It is the 220th object in Halton Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.

objects.name: Centaurus A
objects.why: The nearest large radio galaxy: a giant elliptical crossed by a thick dust lane — the remains of a spiral it swallowed — with jets from its central black hole reaching far beyond the visible galaxy.
unknown: When and how the merger that gave it its dust lane happened.
What shapes its enormous radio lobes, which extend far beyond the galaxy itself.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: Centaurus A is a galaxy in the constellation of Centaurus. It was discovered in 1826 by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop from his home in Parramatta, in New South Wales, Australia. There is considerable debate in the literature regarding the galaxy's fundamental properties such as its Hubble type and distance. It is the closest radio galaxy to Earth, as well as the closest BL Lac object, so its active galactic nucleus has been extensively studied by professional astronomers. The galaxy is also the fifth-brightest in the sky, making it an ideal amateur astronomy target. It is only visible from the southern hemisphere and low northern latitudes.

objects.name: I Zwicky 18
objects.why: A dwarf galaxy with some of the most chemically pristine gas known — very little of the elements heavier than helium that stars make — almost like the gas left by the Big Bang.
unknown: Whether it is truly young. It was once thought to be forming its first stars; Hubble later found older ones, but how old they are is still debated.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: I Zwicky 18 is a blue compact dwarf and Wolf–Rayet galaxy located about 18.44 megaparsecs away in the constellation Ursa Major. The galaxy was first identified by Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky in a 1930s photographic survey of galaxies. It also possesses an active galactic nucleus.

objects.name: Leo P
objects.why: A tiny gas-rich dwarf galaxy found in 2013 from the radio glow of its hydrogen, just beyond the Local Group, with some of the most pristine gas known.
unknown: How a galaxy this small held on to its gas and kept forming stars, when the radiation of the early universe should have stopped it.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: Leo P is a small, star-forming irregular galaxy located in the constellation Leo, discovered through the blind HI Arecibo Legacy Fast ALFA (ALFALFA) survey, as an ultra-compact high-velocity cloud (UCHVC) of hydrogen gas. Its confirmation as a dwarf galaxy in 2013 suggests that other such UCHVCs are possibly undiscovered dwarf galaxies themselves. Leo P is noteworthy for harbouring one of the most metal-poor environments in the local universe. Its metallicity is just 3% that of the Sun's, meaning that its stars contain 30 times less heavy elements than the Sun. This makes Leo P similar to the pristine environments of primordial galaxies.

objects.name: Segue 1
objects.why: One of the faintest galaxies known, with only around a thousand stars, orbiting the Milky Way — yet its stars move as if held by far more mass than they have: it seems to be mostly dark matter.
unknown: Whether it is really a dark-matter-dominated dwarf galaxy, or a star cluster being torn apart.
If it is a dwarf, it is one of the best places to look for signals from dark matter particles.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: Segue 1 is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy or globular cluster situated in the constellation Leo and discovered in 2006 by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. It is located at a distance of about 23 kpc from the Sun and moves away from the Sun with a velocity of about 206 km/s. Segue 1 has a noticeably elongated shape with a half-light radius of about 30 pc. This elongation may be caused by tidal forces from the Milky Way galaxy if Segue 1 is being disrupted now.

objects.name: Sagittarius Dwarf
objects.why: A small galaxy being torn apart by the Milky Way. Its stars are strung out in a stream that wraps all the way round the sky. It lies behind the Galaxy's centre, so a photo shows only Milky Way stars in front of it.
unknown: How much it has shaped the Milky Way: its passes through the disk may have triggered bursts of star formation and ripples in the disk.
How massive it was before the Milky Way started stripping it.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, also known as the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy, is an elliptical loop-shaped satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It contains four globular clusters in its main body, with the brightest of them — NGC 6715 (M54) — known well before the discovery of the galaxy itself in 1994. Sgr dSph is roughly 10,000 light-years in diameter, and is currently about 80,380 light-years from Earth, travelling in a polar orbit at a distance of about 50,000 light-years from the core of the Milky Way. In its looping, spiraling path, it has passed through the plane of the Milky Way several times in the past. In 2018, the Gaia project of the European Space Agency showed that Sgr dSph had caused perturbations in a set of stars near the Milky Way's core, causing unexpected rippling movements of the stars triggered when it moved through the Milky Way between 300 and 900 million years ago.

objects.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
objects.why: The Milky Way's largest satellite galaxy, visible to the naked eye from the south, with satellites of its own.
unknown: Whether this is its first approach to the Milky Way, or it has passed before.
Its total mass — estimates have grown in recent years — and how much its pull is bending the Milky Way's disk and halo.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is a dwarf galaxy and satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. At a distance of around 50 kiloparsecs, the LMC is the second- or third-closest galaxy to the Milky Way, after the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal and the possible dwarf irregular galaxy called the Canis Major Overdensity. It is about 9.86 kiloparsecs across and has roughly one-hundredth the mass of the Milky Way, making it the fourth-largest galaxy in the Local Group after the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Milky Way, and the Triangulum Galaxy (M33).

objects.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
objects.why: The Large Cloud's smaller partner, joined to it by a bridge of gas and badly distorted by both it and the Milky Way.
unknown: Its true shape: it is stretched out along our line of sight, and a 2024 study suggested it may be two separate objects, one behind the other.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) is a dwarf galaxy near the Milky Way. Classified as a dwarf irregular galaxy, the SMC has a D25 isophotal diameter of about 5.78 kiloparsecs (18,900 light-years), and contains several hundred million stars. It has a total mass of approximately 7 billion solar masses. At a distance of about 200,000 light-years, the SMC is among the nearest intergalactic neighbors of the Milky Way and is one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye.

objects.name: Stephan's Quintet
objects.why: Five galaxies close together in the sky. Four are a real, interacting group; the fifth, NGC 7320, is in the foreground, several times nearer.
unknown: How the giant shock wave between the galaxies — one galaxy is crashing through the group's gas at high speed — formed and what it will do.
How and when the group will merge.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0215 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Stephan's Quintet is a visual grouping of five galaxies in the constellation Pegasus, four of which form a physical association, known as the Hickson Compact Group 92. It was the first compact galaxy group to be discovered and one of the most heavily studied compact galaxy groups. The group was discovered by Édouard Stephan in 1877 using the 80 cm reflector telescope at the Marseille Observatory. The brightest member of the apparent grouping, NGC 7320, while the brightest member of the physical association is NGC 7318B.

objects.name: NGC 6240
objects.why: Galaxies in a late stage of merging, with two active supermassive black holes a few thousand light-years apart.
unknown: Whether there is a third black hole: a 2020 study reported three nuclei.
When the black holes will spiral together and merge.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0243 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: NGC 6240, also known as the Starfish Galaxy, is a nearby ultraluminous infrared galaxy (ULIRG) in the constellation Ophiuchus. It was discovered by French astronomer Édouard Stephan on 12 July 1871.

objects.name: 3C 273
objects.why: The first quasar identified (1963): a feeding black hole so bright it outshines its whole galaxy, billions of light-years away, with a jet long enough to see in ordinary photographs.
unknown: How its jet stays so narrow over hundreds of thousands of light-years.
The details of its host galaxy, lost in the glare.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.1583 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: 3C 273 is a quasar located at the center of a giant elliptical galaxy in the constellation of Virgo. It was the first quasar ever to be identified and is the visually brightest quasar in the sky as seen from the Earth, with an apparent visual magnitude of 12.9, outshining by more than 16 times the entire galaxy that hosts it. The derived distance to this object is 749 megaparsecs. The mass of its central supermassive black hole is approximately 900 million times the mass of the Sun.

objects.name: Cygnus A
objects.why: One of the brightest radio sources in the sky: a galaxy whose black hole drives jets into two huge radio lobes far outside it.
unknown: A bright new radio source appeared near its centre in observations from the 2010s — possibly a second black hole, possibly a flare — and it hasn't been explained.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0562 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Cygnus A is a radio galaxy, one of the strongest radio sources in the sky.

objects.name: Holmberg 15A
objects.why: The central galaxy of the cluster Abell 85, whose black hole was measured in 2019 at about 40 billion solar masses — among the largest known.
unknown: How black holes grew this large.
Why its core is so large and faint; one idea is that stars were flung out by two merging black holes.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: Holmberg 15A is a supergiant elliptical galaxy and the brightest galaxy of the Abell 85 galaxy cluster in the constellation Cetus, about 241.4 megaparsecs from Earth. It was discovered c. 1937 by Erik Holmberg. It became well known when it was reported to have the largest core ever observed in a galaxy, spanning some 15,000 light years, however this was subsequently refuted.

objects.name: ESO 137-001
objects.why: A 'jellyfish' galaxy falling into the Norma cluster at high speed: the cluster's hot gas is stripping the galaxy's own gas away into long tails, where new stars are forming.
unknown: How many stars form in the stripped tails, and how soon the galaxy will run out of gas and stop forming stars.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0155 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: ESO 137-001, also known as the Jellyfish Galaxy, is a barred spiral galaxy located in the constellation Triangulum Australe and in the cluster Abell 3627. As the galaxy moves to the center of the galaxy cluster at 1900 km/s, it is stripped by hot gas, thus creating a 260,000 light-year long tail. This is called ram pressure stripping (RPS). The intergalactic gas in Abell 3627 is at 100 million Kelvin, which causes star formation in the tails. The galaxy has a low amount of Hl regions which combine to a total mass of 3.5x10^8 solar masses, only 10% of which is located in the main disk of ESO 137-001.

objects.name: Hanny's Voorwerp
objects.why: A huge glowing cloud of gas next to the galaxy IC 2497, found in 2007 by Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel on the Galaxy Zoo website. It glows because a quasar in IC 2497 lit it up — but the quasar seems to have faded since. The photo is centred on IC 2497.
unknown: Why the quasar switched off so quickly, within the time it took its light to cross to the cloud.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0500 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Hanny's Voorwerp is an instance of an astronomical phenomenon called a quasar ionization echo. It was discovered in 2007 by Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel while she was participating as a volunteer in the Galaxy Zoo project, part of the Zooniverse group of citizen science websites. Photographically, it appears as a bright blob close to spiral galaxy IC 2497 in the constellation Leo Minor.

objects.name: Rubin's Galaxy (UGC 2885)
objects.why: A giant spiral about two and a half times as wide as the Milky Way, nicknamed after Vera Rubin, who studied it while gathering evidence for dark matter.
unknown: How it grew so large so quietly, apparently without major collisions.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: UGC 2885, Rubin's Galaxy, or the Godzilla galaxy is a giant barred spiral galaxy of type SA(rs)c in the constellation Perseus. It is 84 megaparsecs from Earth and measures 134.3 kiloparsecs across, making it one of the largest known spiral galaxies. It is also a possible member of the Perseus–Pisces Supercluster.

objects.name: Canis Major Dwarf
objects.why: A patch of extra stars below the plane of the Milky Way, announced in 2003 as the nearest galaxy to us. The photo shows only Milky Way stars.
unknown: Whether it is a galaxy at all, or just the warped, flared outer edge of the Milky Way's own disk seen from an angle — still argued.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Canis Major Overdensity or Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy is a disputed dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Group, located in the same part of the sky as the constellation Canis Major.

objects.name: Bullet Cluster
objects.why: Two clusters of galaxies that collided. Their hot gas, seen in X-rays, was slowed by the crash, while most of the mass — mapped by how it bends light from galaxies behind — passed straight through: some of the strongest evidence that dark matter exists.
unknown: Whether a collision this fast is too unlikely in the standard picture of the universe.
What the dark matter is made of.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.2966 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: The Bullet Cluster consists of two colliding clusters of galaxies. Strictly speaking, the name Bullet Cluster refers to the smaller subcluster, moving away from the larger one. It is at a comoving radial distance of 1.141 Gpc. The first known reference to this cluster comes from a 1992 paper titled, "The Einstein Slew Survey".

objects.name: Seyfert's Sextet
objects.why: A tight group that looks like six galaxies: four are interacting, one is a much more distant background galaxy, and the 'sixth' is a tail of stars torn from one of the others.
unknown: How soon the four will merge into a single galaxy.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0148 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Seyfert's Sextet is a compact group of galaxies located approximately 190 million light-years away in the constellation Serpens. The core interacting group spans approximately 35,000 light-years across, making the system smaller than the disk of the Milky Way. The members exhibit an average recessional velocity of 4,350 km/s. High-resolution imaging by the Hubble Space Telescope confirmed that the group consists of four physically interacting galaxies, one prominent tidal stream, and one background spiral galaxy positioned along the same line of sight.

objects.name: Fornax A
objects.why: A giant galaxy with shells and ripples of stars — signs it swallowed smaller galaxies — and a black hole powering two radio lobes much larger than the visible galaxy.
unknown: When the mergers happened and which one fed the black hole that made the radio lobes.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: NGC 1316 is a lenticular galaxy about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax. It is a radio galaxy and at 1400 MHz the fourth-brightest radio source in the sky. It was discovered by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop on 2 September 1826.

objects.name: Hercules A
objects.why: A galaxy whose central black hole drives some of the most powerful radio jets known, spanning far more than the visible galaxy.
unknown: Why its jets show bright rings along their length — possibly repeated outbursts from the black hole.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.1550 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: Hercules A, or 3C 348, is a bright astronomical radio source galaxy in the constellation Hercules. It is an elliptical galaxy, and the origin of one of the largest known astronomical radio sources, emanating 459,820 light years on either side of its point of origin, making the feature nearly a million light years across. Hercules A was first catalogued by astronomers at the University of Cambridge in April 1961 in a paper published to The Observatory.

objects.name: Tadpole Galaxy
objects.why: A spiral with a single tail of stars hundreds of thousands of light-years long, drawn out by a smaller galaxy that passed close by.
unknown: Where the intruder galaxy is now — it may be behind the spiral, seen through its disk.
objects.distSrc: from its redshift z = 0.0311 (Hubble's law, H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc)
objects.about: The Tadpole Galaxy, also known as UGC 10214 and Arp 188, is a disrupted barred spiral galaxy located 143.6 megaparsecs from Earth in the northern constellation Draco. The first known reference to this galaxy comes from the 1959 Vorontsov-Vel'yaminov Interacting Galaxies catalog, where it was listed as VV 29.

objects.name: Atoms for Peace (NGC 7252)
objects.why: The aftermath of two galaxies merging, with loops and tails of stars around a body that is turning into an elliptical galaxy.
unknown: Whether merger remnants like this really become ordinary elliptical galaxies, as this one seems to be doing.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: NGC 7252 is a peculiar galaxy resulting from an interaction between two galaxies that started a billion years ago. It is located 220 million light years away in the constellation Aquarius. It is also called Atoms for Peace Galaxy, a nickname which comes from its loop-like structure, made of stars, that resembles a classic diagram of an electron orbiting an atomic nucleus.

objects.name: Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte
objects.why: A dwarf galaxy on the lonely edge of the Local Group that seems never to have interacted with a big galaxy — a chance to see how a galaxy evolves left alone.
unknown: How it kept forming stars over billions of years with no neighbour to stir it up.
objects.distSrc: NED-D: median of the published redshift-independent distances
objects.about: The Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte Galaxy (WLM) is a barred irregular galaxy discovered in 1909 by Max Wolf, located on the outer edges of the Local Group. The discovery of the nature of the galaxy was accredited to Knut Lundmark and Philibert Jacques Melotte in 1926. It is located in the constellation of Cetus.
